strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification using control theory perspective (P-controller vs PI-controller analogy)
Strong experimental results with substantial improvements (up to +5.95 dB PSNR on LACT-90, 3.3× convergence speedup)
Thorough experimental validation with comprehensive baselines, multiple modalities, and good ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component
Theoretically grounded approach with rigorous fixed-point characterization (Theorem D.2) showing optimality conditions of dual-coupled solutions
Creative and practical Spectral Homogenization solution that elegantly bridges optimization rigor with diffusion model statistical requirements
Controlled comparison with DiffPIR using identical data-consistency operators ensures fair evaluation
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (particularly Figure 3) and detailed algorithmic descriptions
weaknesses: Incomplete convergence theory: paper acknowledges global convergence guarantees remain open problem; only fixed-point analysis provided, which is weaker than convergence guarantees claimed in abstract

Spectral Homogenization justification relies on strong assumptions (dominance condition Eq. 20: artifact sparsity ≫ error sparsity) that may not hold throughout iterations, especially early on; only second-order moment matching guaranteed by Proposition 3.1

Bootstrap residual estimation (r = v - z^{k}) conflates structured artifacts with denoising error; early iterations when z^{k} is far from ground truth could be problematic despite theoretical justification in Appendix B
Limited experimental scope: single dataset per modality (AbdomenCT-1K for CT, fastMRI knee for MRI) with small test sets (6 patients, 96 slices); generalization to other anatomies/protocols unclear
Images limited to 256×256 (CT) and 320×320 (MRI); performance on clinical-resolution images unknown

Trade-off with perceptual quality: LPIPS scores comparable or sometimes worse than baselines, indicating prioritization of physical fidelity over perceptual metrics; this important trade-off underexplored
Absence of clinical validation, user studies, or radiologist evaluation; medical imaging claims require clinical validation before deployment

Limited novelty: primarily combines known techniques (classical ADMM dual variables + established diffusion priors); Spectral Homogenization, while novel, feels incremental (frequency-domain filtering is well-understood)
Incomplete sensitivity analysis: missing ablations on hyperparameters (kernel bandwidth δ, penalty parameter ρ), computational overhead of SH, and wall-clock time costs
Theoretical assumption of denoiser-as-proximal operator (D.1) may not perfectly hold for pretrained models; how violations affect theory not discussed

strengths: Well-motivated core insight: identifies that memoryless PnP solvers suffer steady-state bias; control theory perspective (P vs PI controllers) is compelling and intuitive

Novel technical integration: Spectral Homogenization module elegantly adapts structured dual residuals into AWGN-compatible inputs without retraining; filling spectral valleys preserves semantic content
Strong empirical results on CT: +4.76 dB LACT-90, +2.69 dB SVCT-20, approximately 3× efficiency gain at matched quality; substantial and clinically meaningful improvements

Rigorous experimental validation: multiple datasets/tasks, controlled comparison with DiffPIR, clean ablations isolating contributions (dual +4.55 dB, SH +0.15 dB), spectral mechanism verification, negligible computational overhead

Solid theoretical foundation: Theorem E.2 characterizes fixed-point optimality, Theorem E.3 identifies systematic bias in loosely-coupled methods, Proposition 4.1 provides moment-matching justification for SH

Comprehensive presentation: clear positioning vs concurrent work, excellent illustrative figures, 30-page appendix with detailed proofs/implementation/additional experiments, broad applicability demonstrated on natural images
Strong reproducibility: detailed algorithm descriptions, hyperparameter specifications for all baselines, dataset documentation, framework specification; code release promised
Honest limitations discussion: clearly identifies scope constraints (2D, 256×256, explicit A required), explains modality-dependent gain variations (CT >> MRI due to structured artifact geometry)
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: fixed-point analysis assumes denoiser acts as proximal operator (Assumption E.1), which pretrained diffusion models don't strictly satisfy; analysis is motivational rather than rigorous; no global convergence guarantee established

SH theoretical justification incomplete: Proposition 4.1 assumes phase uniformly distributed and independent of residual, which may not hold; bootstrap residual estimation (r = v - z) uses imperfect z as proxy for clean signal, creating circular reasoning (using imperfect estimate to correct imperfection), though Appendix C's spectral separability argument partially addresses this

Modest MRI improvements limit impact: fastMRI brain AF=10 shows +2.24 dB, knee AF=10 shows +0.94 dB only; single-coil MRI setup less clinically typical than multi-coil; improvements partially masked by noise rather than addressing measurement fidelity directly

Limited experimental scope: only 2D images (256×256); scalability to 3D volumetric reconstruction common in clinical practice is unclear; concurrent 2026 submissions (Park et al., Shrestha & Fu, Bendel et al.) reduce novelty margin
Informal treatment of key concepts: 'approximately flat spectrum', 'statistically compliant pseudo-AWGN', and 'spectral valleys' not formally defined; makes SH mechanism understanding imprecise
Incomplete code availability: repository link missing from manuscript ('available at' without URL); reproducibility dependent on external code release
Incomplete theoretical analysis: SH perturbation effects on fixed-point properties not analyzed; no convergence rate analysis; Theorem E.2 only valid under unrealistic denoiser assumption
